question: What are the most important Spring annotations every developer should know?
title: Essential Spring Annotations Overview

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing web annotations but not configuration or lifecycle annotations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Organize annotations by category and explain the purpose of each group

sections.title: Spring Annotation Categories
sections.content:
**Configuration**:
- `@Configuration` — class is a source of bean definitions
- `@Bean` — method produces a bean
- `@ComponentScan` — enable component scanning
- `@PropertySource` — load .properties file into Environment

**Stereotypes**:
- `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, `@RestController`

**Injection**:
- `@Autowired` — inject by type
- `@Qualifier` — disambiguate by name
- `@Value("${key}")` — inject property value
- `@Primary` — default bean when multiple match

**Lifecycle**:
- `@PostConstruct`, `@PreDestroy`

**Conditional**:
- `@Profile`, `@Conditional`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `@SpringBootApplication` = `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`
- `@Value` injects single properties; `@ConfigurationProperties` for grouped
- `@Transactional` (Spring Data) manages database transactions
- `@Async` makes a method run asynchronously
- `@Scheduled(cron="...")` schedules recurring tasks
- `@EventListener` listens for Spring events

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd group Spring annotations into categories. For configuration, the key ones are `@Configuration` for bean factory classes, `@Bean` for factory methods, and `@ComponentScan` for enabling auto-detection. For stereotypes, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, and `@RestController` mark the layer each class belongs to. For injection, `@Autowired` injects beans by type and `@Value` injects property values from your properties file. For lifecycle, `@PostConstruct` runs initialization after injection and `@PreDestroy` runs cleanup. And `@Transactional` from Spring Data is essential for database operations. Knowing this organized view shows you understand the architecture, not just individual annotations.

seo.metaTitle: Essential Spring Annotations Overview | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Complete overview of important Spring annotations organized by category: configuration, stereotypes, injection, lifecycle, and conditional annotations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Knowing one annotation isn't enough — interviewers want to see that you understand how annotation groups fit together to build a Spring application.

beats.text: Spring annotations fall into five groups: configuration (how beans are defined), stereotypes (which layer a class belongs to), injection (how dependencies arrive), lifecycle (initialization and cleanup hooks), and conditional (when beans are created). Knowing the groups — not just individual annotations — shows you understand Spring's architecture.

Spring uses annotations to replace XML configuration. Each annotation group replaces a different section of the old XML: bean definitions, component declarations, property injection, lifecycle callbacks, and environment-specific config. The annotation model is the same set of concerns — just expressed closer to the code.

items: Configuration: @Configuration, @Bean, @ComponentScan, @PropertySource. Defines the bean factory and scanning strategy.
Stereotypes: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController. Registers classes as beans and communicates layer.
Injection: @Autowired, @Qualifier, @Value, @Primary. Controls how dependencies and properties flow into beans.
Lifecycle: @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy. Hooks for initialization after injection and cleanup before shutdown.
Conditional: @Profile, @Conditional, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnClass. Controls which beans are created per environment.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, @SpringBootApplication on the main class combines @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan — it's a convenience annotation that wires up three groups at once. OrderService has @Service (stereotype) and @Transactional (transaction management). It @Autowires UserRepository (injection) and reads a config value with @Value (injection). Its @PostConstruct validates the config at startup. non-obvious: @Transactional isn't strictly in a single group — it's an AOP-based annotation that wraps method execution in a database transaction. It's worth mentioning separately.

items: Don't memorize annotations without their category — explaining that @Repository is a stereotype annotation that also adds exception translation is more impressive than listing annotations.
Don't forget lifecycle annotations — @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy are commonly overlooked but frequently tested.

speakable_v2.cap: Organize your answer around groups — configuration, stereotypes, injection, lifecycle, conditional — and you demonstrate architecture understanding, not just annotation trivia.
followup_handoff: What does @SpringBootApplication expand to and what does each component annotation do?

question: What is @Value annotation in Spring?
title: @Value Annotation in Spring Explained
direct_answer: **`@Value`** injects values into Spring bean fields or constructor parameters. It supports property values (`@Value("${server.port}")`), SpEL expressions (`@Value("#{2 * 5}")`), and default values (`@Value("${key:default}")`). It reads from `application.properties` and the Spring Environment.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the ${} vs #{} difference — properties vs SpEL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between ${} for property values and #{} for SpEL expressions

sections.title: @Value Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`${property.key}`**: reads from properties/environment
- **`#{SpEL expression}`**: evaluates Spring Expression Language
- **`${key:default}`**: default value if property not set
- Supports type conversion: String → int, boolean, List<String>
- Comma-separated values → `List<String>` automatically
- Not suitable for grouped properties — use `@ConfigurationProperties` instead

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Value` is the annotation for injecting configuration values into Spring beans. The most common use is `@Value("${property.key}")` which reads a value from `application.properties`. You can set a default with a colon: `@Value("${key:defaultValue}")`. Spring handles type conversion automatically — if the property value is `8080`, it can inject it into an `int` field. There's also a SpEL syntax using `#{...}` for Spring Expression Language which lets you do computations or call Java methods. For more than two or three related properties, `@ConfigurationProperties` is a cleaner approach than multiple `@Value` annotations.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Value with ${} and #{}?
How do you inject a list from application.properties?
When should you use @ConfigurationProperties instead of @Value?

seo.metaTitle: @Value Annotation Spring Explained | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Value annotation injects property values and SpEL expressions in Spring beans with default values and type conversion support.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Value is how a Spring bean reads from application.properties — one annotation, and a config value lands directly in a field.

beats.text: @Value injects values from the Spring Environment into bean fields or constructor parameters. It supports two syntaxes: ${property.key} reads from application.properties or any loaded property source, and #{SpEL expression} evaluates a Spring Expression Language expression. You can also provide a default with ${key:defaultValue} — if the property isn't set, the default is used instead.

Hard-coding configuration values in code makes deployment inflexible. @Value externalizes them to application.properties, environment variables, or any property source. You change the value in one place and every bean that injects it picks up the new value without recompiling.

items: ${property.key}: reads a string value from the environment. Spring auto-converts to int, boolean, or List<String>.
${key:default}: uses the default if the key isn't in any property source.
#{SpEL}: evaluates Spring Expression Language — call Java methods, reference other beans, do arithmetic.
Type conversion: a comma-separated string like a,b,c can be injected directly into List<String>.
Limitation: use @ConfigurationProperties instead when you have more than two or three related properties — it's cleaner and type-safe.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, AppService reads three values: @Value("${server.port}") int port reads the port as an int automatically. @Value("${app.feature.enabled:true}") boolean featureEnabled defaults to true if the property is absent. @Value("${app.admin.emails}") List<String> adminEmails splits a comma-separated value into a list. gotcha: @Value doesn't work in static fields or in @Configuration methods that are called before the environment is loaded. Use it in regular Spring-managed beans.

items: Don't use @Value for a large group of related properties — define a @ConfigurationProperties class instead for type safety and IDE completion.
Don't forget to add quotes inside the string: @Value("${my.key}") — missing the dollar-brace syntax results in the literal string being injected instead of the property value.

speakable_v2.cap: @Value is for single property injection — when you have a cluster of related properties, @ConfigurationProperties is the cleaner alternative.
followup_handoff: How does @ConfigurationProperties differ from multiple @Value annotations for grouped config?
What happens at startup if a @Value property key doesn't exist and no default is provided?

question: What is @Profile in Spring and when do you use it?
title: @Profile Annotation in Spring Explained
direct_answer: **`@Profile("dev")`** on a bean or configuration class means that bean is only created when the `dev` profile is active. Use it to provide different implementations for dev, test, and prod — like an in-memory data store for dev and a real database for prod.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @Profile on beans with profile-specific properties files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example: different DataSource implementations per profile

sections.title: @Profile Bean Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Profile("dev")` — bean created only when `dev` profile is active
- `@Profile("!prod")` — created when NOT in prod
- `@Profile({"dev", "test"})` — active in dev OR test
- Complementary to `application-{profile}.properties` — profiles work together
- `@Configuration @Profile` — entire config class conditional
- Useful for: different data sources, mock vs real services, feature flags

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Profile` is a conditional annotation that controls whether a bean is created based on the active Spring profile. A classic use case is having two `DataSource` beans: one annotated `@Profile("dev")` that uses H2 in-memory database for local development, and another `@Profile("prod")` that connects to the real MySQL. Activate the right one with `spring.profiles.active=dev` or the runtime flag. You can also put `@Profile` on an entire `@Configuration` class to conditionally load all its beans. It works alongside profile-specific properties files — together they give you complete environment-specific configuration.

followup_questions: How do you combine multiple profiles?

seo.metaTitle: @Profile Annotation Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how Spring @Profile annotation creates beans conditionally based on active profile for dev/prod environment-specific configuration.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Profile is the switch that turns a bean on or off depending on where your app is running.

beats.text: @Profile is a conditional annotation that makes a bean exist only when a specific profile is active. Annotate a bean or @Configuration class with @Profile("dev") and it's only created when the dev profile is active. All other profiles don't see that bean at all. Activate profiles with spring.profiles.active in application.properties or as a command-line argument.

Dev, test, and prod environments need different infrastructure. You don't want H2 in-memory in production or a live payment gateway in development. @Profile lets you define which bean implementation wins per environment without if-statements in your code.

items: @Profile("dev"): bean created only when dev is active.
@Profile("!prod"): bean created when the prod profile is NOT active — useful for dev and test without listing both.
@Profile({"dev", "test"}): active in either dev or test.
On @Configuration class: all @Bean methods in that class are conditional on the profile.
On @Component class: that service is only registered when the profile is active.
Complements application-{profile}.properties: @Profile controls which beans exist; profile-specific properties files control their config values.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DevConfig is @Configuration @Profile("dev"). It defines a DataSource bean that creates an H2 in-memory database. ProdConfig is @Configuration @Profile("prod") and defines a HikariCP DataSource pointing to MySQL. Running with spring.profiles.active=dev activates H2. Deploying to production with spring.profiles.active=prod activates MySQL. OrderService doesn't know or care — it just @Autowires DataSource. non-obvious: @Profile can also guard @Component classes directly. @Profile("dev") on a mock payment service means it only exists in dev — a real PaymentService is active in prod.

items: Don't confuse @Profile on beans with profile-specific application-dev.properties files — both use profiles but serve different purposes.
If no bean matches the active profile for a required injection, Spring throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup — always make sure there's a matching implementation for every active profile.

speakable_v2.cap: @Profile is your environment gate — one annotation flips which bean exists without any conditional code in your services.
followup_handoff: How do @Profile and application-dev.properties work together for full environment-specific configuration?
What happens if a required @Autowired bean only exists in a profile that isn't active?

question: What is @PropertySource in Spring?
title: @PropertySource in Spring Explained
direct_answer: **`@PropertySource("classpath:myconfig.properties")`** loads a properties file into the Spring `Environment`. Values from the file can then be injected with `@Value("${key}")`. It's used to load additional properties files beyond the default `application.properties`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @PropertySource with application.properties — Boot loads application.properties automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you need @PropertySource vs just using application.properties

sections.title: @PropertySource Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@PropertySource` loads ADDITIONAL properties files into Spring Environment
- Spring Boot auto-loads `application.properties` — no annotation needed for it
- Multiple files: `@PropertySources({@PropertySource("classpath:a.properties"), @PropertySource("classpath:b.properties")})`
- Use `ignoreResourceNotFound=true` if file is optional
- YAML files not supported by `@PropertySource` — use application.yml for YAML
- Typical use: separate concerns (db.properties, mail.properties) for organization

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@PropertySource` loads an additional properties file into the Spring Environment, making its key-value pairs available via `@Value`. Spring Boot automatically loads `application.properties`, so you don't need `@PropertySource` for that. You'd use it when you want to organize configuration into multiple files — like `database.properties`, `mail.properties`, `security.properties` — and load them into specific configuration classes. Note that `@PropertySource` doesn't support YAML format. If you want multiple property sources in Spring Boot, you typically stick with profiles and profile-specific property files rather than `@PropertySource`.

followup_questions: What is the order of property source loading in Spring Boot?

seo.metaTitle: @PropertySource Spring Annotation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @PropertySource loads additional properties files into Spring Environment for use with @Value injection beyond application.properties.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot auto-loads application.properties — @PropertySource is for when you want to load additional property files beyond that default.

beats.text: @PropertySource is a class-level annotation on @Configuration classes that loads an additional .properties file into the Spring Environment. Once loaded, all keys in that file are available via @Value and Environment.getProperty(). Spring Boot loads application.properties automatically without needing @PropertySource — this annotation is for supplementary files you want to load on top.

Large applications sometimes want to separate configuration by concern — one file for database settings, another for mail settings, another for security. @PropertySource lets you load each file into the matching @Configuration class, keeping config co-located with the code that uses it.

items: Basic: @PropertySource("classpath:myfile.properties") loads the file from src/main/resources into the Environment.
Optional file: @PropertySource(value="classpath:optional.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound=true) — no error if the file doesn't exist.
Multiple files: @PropertySources({@PropertySource("classpath:a.properties"), @PropertySource("classpath:b.properties")}).
YAML not supported: @PropertySource works only with .properties format. Use application.yml or application-{profile}.yml for YAML.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DatabaseConfig is annotated @Configuration @PropertySource("classpath:database.properties"). The file contains db.url and db.username. DatabaseConfig reads them with @Value and uses them in the DataSource @Bean method. non-obvious: in modern Spring Boot projects, this pattern is rare — application.properties and profile-specific properties files handle most cases. You'd reach for @PropertySource mainly when integrating with a legacy system that has its own named properties files you can't rename.

items: @PropertySource doesn't support YAML files — if you pass a .yml file, it silently loads nothing or throws a parse error.
Property source order matters — if the same key exists in application.properties and a @PropertySource file, the one loaded last wins unless you configure precedence.

speakable_v2.cap: @PropertySource is rarely needed in modern Spring Boot — application.properties plus profiles covers most scenarios. Know it for legacy integration.

question: What is @Conditional in Spring and how does it work?
title: @Conditional Annotation in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Conditional(MyCondition.class)`** creates a bean only when a custom condition is met. `MyCondition` implements `Condition` interface and its `matches()` method returns true/false. Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built on `@Conditional` variants like `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of conditional bean creation mechanics
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the common @Conditional variants provided by Spring Boot
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: List the Spring Boot @Conditional variants and what each checks

sections.title: @Conditional Variants in Spring Boot
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides many built-in `@Conditional` annotations:

- **`@ConditionalOnClass(Foo.class)`**: create if class is on classpath
- **`@ConditionalOnMissingClass`**: create if class is NOT on classpath
- **`@ConditionalOnBean(Foo.class)`**: create if bean of type exists
- **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`**: create if no bean of type exists
- **`@ConditionalOnProperty(name="feature", havingValue="true")`**: create if property matches
- **`@ConditionalOnWebApplication`**: create if running in a web context
- **`@ConditionalOnExpression("#{...}")`**: create if SpEL expression is true

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Conditional` is the base; Spring Boot ships convenience variants
- Auto-configuration classes use `@Conditional` to be non-invasive
- You can stack multiple conditions — all must pass
- Custom condition: implement `Condition` interface, return true/false from `matches()`
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` is great for feature flags in properties
- Evaluated during context refresh — after all bean definitions are loaded

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Conditional` is the foundation of Spring Boot's auto-configuration. It allows bean creation to be gated by a condition. The base `@Conditional` takes a class that implements the `Condition` interface and calls its `matches()` method. Spring Boot ships with many ready-made variants: `@ConditionalOnClass` activates when a specific class is on the classpath, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` activates when no bean of a type exists, and `@ConditionalOnProperty` activates when a specific property has a specific value. The last one is very useful for feature flags — set `feature.new-ui.enabled=true` in properties and the new UI bean activates. All of Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built on these conditionals.

followup_questions: How would you write a custom @Conditional condition?

seo.metaTitle: @Conditional Spring Annotation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Conditional and its Spring Boot variants like @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnProperty power conditional bean creation.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Conditional is the engine under Spring Boot's magic — every auto-configuration class uses it to decide whether to create beans or stay out of the way.

beats.text: @Conditional gates bean creation behind a runtime check. The base annotation takes a class that implements the Condition interface and whose matches() method returns true or false. If it returns true, the bean is created. Spring Boot ships dozens of convenience variants built on top of @Conditional, each checking a specific thing — classpath, existing beans, property values, web context.

Spring Boot's auto-configuration is non-invasive by design. It creates beans only when you haven't defined your own. @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the key — Spring Boot says 'create this default bean only if the user hasn't already registered one.' You override auto-configuration by registering your own bean, and Spring Boot's disappears.

items: @ConditionalOnClass: create if a specific class is on the classpath — used by auto-configs for optional libraries.
@ConditionalOnMissingBean: create only if no bean of that type is already registered — the auto-configuration override mechanism.
@ConditionalOnProperty(name, havingValue): create if a property has a specific value — the feature flag mechanism.
@ConditionalOnWebApplication: create only in a web app context.
Custom condition: implement Condition, return true/false from matches(ConditionContext, AnnotatedTypeMetadata).

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, we want a beta feature toggle. We add beta.feature.enabled=true to application.properties in dev. The BetaFeatureService @Bean method carries @ConditionalOnProperty(name="beta.feature.enabled", havingValue="true"). In dev, the bean is created and active. In prod where the property is false or absent, the bean doesn't exist and the feature is off — zero code changes between environments. non-obvious: @ConditionalOnMissingBean is why you can override Spring Boot's default ObjectMapper — define your own @Bean ObjectMapper and Spring Boot's auto-configured one backs off.

items: Don't use @Conditional for things @Profile already handles — use @Profile for environment-specific beans and @Conditional for logic-driven conditions.
Multiple @Conditional annotations on one bean are AND-ed — all conditions must pass. If you need OR logic, write a custom Condition class.

speakable_v2.cap: @Conditional is how Spring Boot stays non-invasive — learn @ConditionalOnMissingBean and @ConditionalOnProperty and you'll understand 80% of auto-configuration.

question: What is @Transactional in Spring and what does it do?
title: @Transactional in Spring Explained
direct_answer: **`@Transactional`** marks a method (or class) to run within a database transaction. Spring wraps the method in a proxy that begins a transaction before the method runs and commits it on success or rolls back on unchecked exception. It eliminates manual `begin/commit/rollback` code.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Transactional only works on public methods, or that it requires Spring proxy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain rollback rules: rolls back on RuntimeException by default, not checked exceptions

sections.title: How @Transactional Works
Key Points
sections.content:
- Only works on `public` methods (Spring proxy limitation)
- Calling `@Transactional` from within the same class bypasses the proxy (self-invocation problem)
- `rollbackFor = Exception.class` to roll back on checked exceptions too
- `readOnly = true` optimization for read-only queries
- `propagation` controls nested transaction behavior (REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, etc.)
- `isolation` controls transaction isolation level
- Spring Data JPA: `save()`, `delete()` are `@Transactional` by default

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Transactional` manages database transactions declaratively. When you annotate a service method with it, Spring wraps the method in a proxy that opens a transaction before calling the method and either commits on success or rolls back if a `RuntimeException` is thrown. This eliminates the manual try-catch-finally pattern for transaction management. Two important gotchas: first, it only works on public methods because Spring's proxy can only intercept public calls. Second, if you call a `@Transactional` method from within the same class, the proxy is bypassed and no transaction is started — this is the self-invocation problem. Also worth knowing: it rolls back automatically on `RuntimeException` but not checked exceptions by default.

followup_questions: Why doesn't @Transactional work on private methods?
What is the self-invocation problem with @Transactional?
What is transaction propagation in Spring?

seo.metaTitle: @Transactional Spring Annotation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Transactional works in Spring for declarative transaction management, rollback rules, and common gotchas like self-invocation and private methods.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Transactional wraps your method in a database transaction — success commits, RuntimeException rolls back, and you never write begin/commit/rollback code again.

beats.text: @Transactional marks a method to run inside a database transaction. Spring wraps the annotated class in a proxy. When the method is called, the proxy opens a transaction, calls the real method, and commits on success. If a RuntimeException is thrown, the proxy rolls back. Checked exceptions don't trigger rollback by default — use rollbackFor=Exception.class to include them.

Without @Transactional you'd write try-catch blocks with manual beginTransaction(), commit(), and rollback() calls around every data operation. @Transactional moves that boilerplate into the framework via AOP, letting your business method focus purely on logic.

items: Default rollback: rolls back on RuntimeException and Error only. Checked exceptions commit by default.
rollbackFor=Exception.class: extends rollback to all exceptions including checked ones.
readOnly=true: hint to the database that this is a read-only transaction — enables optimizations.
propagation: controls what happens when a @Transactional method calls another @Transactional method — REQUIRED (default, reuse existing), REQUIRES_NEW (always start fresh), etc.
Public methods only: Spring's proxy can only intercept public calls — @Transactional on private or package-private methods is silently ignored.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService.placeOrder() is @Transactional. It calls orderRepo.save(order) and inventoryRepo.reduce(order). Both database operations participate in the same transaction. If inventoryRepo.reduce() throws an InsufficientStockException (a RuntimeException), Spring rolls back both operations — the order is never saved. sharp edge: if you call this.placeOrder() from another method inside the same OrderService class, the proxy is bypassed and no transaction is started. That's the self-invocation problem. Inject OrderService into itself or extract the method to a separate bean to fix it.

items: Don't put @Transactional on private methods — Spring's proxy ignores them silently, and you'll wonder why rollback isn't working.
Don't call a @Transactional method from another method in the same class — the proxy is bypassed. Extract the method to a different bean.

speakable_v2.cap: @Transactional is declarative transaction management — know the rollback rules, the public-method requirement, and the self-invocation trap.
followup_handoff: What is transaction propagation and what's the difference between REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW?
